newsitem.title: LEBANON: Lebanon's Hariri faces awkward time with cabinet.
newsitem.headline: Lebanon's Hariri faces awkward time with cabinet.

text.p: Lebanon's Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri began his third term of office on Friday enjoying a strengthened parliamentary base but facing the awkward prospect of opposition from within his own cabinet.
The 30-member government formed on Thursday evening launched a new stage in Hariri's four-year-old drive to rebuild Lebanon that could last until presidential elections in October 1998.
But the team, assembled in two weeks of tough negotiations with President Elias Hrawi and parliament Speaker Nabih Berri, lacks the unity Hariri sought.

It appears to contain the seeds of rivalries similar to those in the billionaire construction tycoon's first government which caused him deep frustration between October 1992 and May 1995 and several times provoked him to threaten resignation.

Despite inclusion of 12 new members, the top portfolios are unchanged and the government lacks outstanding figures likely to bring fresh energy to the job of rebuilding Lebanon after the 1975-90 civil war and resolving pressing economic and social problems coming to the forefront of the agenda.

In fact, two of the most dynamic ministers were dropped -- health minister Marwan Hamade and hard-driving telecommunications minister Al-Fadel Chalak, a close colleague of Hariri, forcing Hariri to take over the telecommunications portfolio himself.

In contrast, several old foes of Hariri returned to the government, two of them outspoken critics he had managed to exclude from the previous cabinet he formed in May 1995 after resigning in protest against opposition he faced in the government as well as in parliament.

Hariri's enemies returned after Hrawi, a Maronite Christian, argued that the government should be politically balanced and represent a broad spectrum of political opinion rather than forming a united front under Hariri.

Hariri's reaction was plain on Thursday night as he emerged from the last round of negotiations with Hrawi and Berri. The normally genial, voluble tycoon brushed past reporters with a glum "no comment".
Other prominent politicians were equally downbeat about the new team.
"This new cabinet did not deserve all that effort," said former prime minister Selim al-Hoss.
"This new cabinet is not up to the political, economic and social challenges," said independent Christian Nasib Lahoud, a prominent deputy with presidential ambitions.

Hariri looked like Lebanon's dominant political figure in September when he won a seat in parliamentary elections and emerged at the head of a big bloc of deputies after an electoral alliance with Berri.

When negotiations on forming the government began, he confidently declared that he wanted a "harmonious" team driven by the common goal of rebuilding Lebanon and that opposition belonged in parliament, not in the government.
But Hrawi and Berri managed to increase the number of their own supporters in the government at Hariri's expense as the prime minister's enemies also returned to office.

The ministers most likely to cause Hariri trouble are Maronite Christian Sleiman Franjieh, Druze Talal Arslane and Greek Catholic Nichola Fattouche, all of whom have opposed Hariri's policies from within previous governments.
But the loudest critic of all at present is Druze leader Walid Jumblatt, hitherto a close Hariri ally who has turned against him, saying he is becoming too powerful.
"We cannot replace the absolute powers of the president with absolute powers of the prime minister," Jumblatt declared at the weekend.
Jumblatt returned to the attack as soon as the government was formed, warning Hariri he faces a battle over the policy statement the government must present to parliament.

Hariri is under pressure to pay more attention to poverty and social issues. He has said these will be the new goverment's priorities but he is also expected to carry on with his multi-billion dollar reconstruction programme.
"Prime Minister Hariri has left no room for reconciliation," declared Jumblatt, who leads the Progressive Socialist Party. "The first battle will be over the government's policy statement.

"Greed in financial matters should be stopped and the opposition will be active inside the cabinet, in which Hariri controls the finance ministry, the telecommunications ministry, the information ministry, justice and transportation," he said.
